claims.text: Rapid melt-spinning at approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s produces an amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy.
The rapidly quenched alloy has high residual internal stresses.
The rapidly quenched alloy has a non-relaxed, far-from-equilibrium structure.
A brief isothermal anneal just below Tg immediately after quenching will produce a relaxed amorphous network with reduced internal stress.
The sub-Tg anneal will make the free-volume distribution more homogeneous.
Limited atomic mobility during a sub-Tg hold relaxes quench-induced stresses and structural defects without activating significant crystallization.
Structural relaxation toward a quasi-equilibrium amorphous state increases resistance to crystallization during reheating.
The sub-Tg annealed alloy will retain more amorphous material during solidification than the as-quenched alloy.
The sub-Tg annealed alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature during reheating than the as-quenched alloy.
Rapidly quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 forms an amorphous phase.
The rapidly quenched amorphous alloy has limited stability during subsequent thermal analysis and undergoes premature or complex crystallization.
A hold too close to or above Tg may initiate crystallization and prevent the intervention from succeeding.
Slow cooling can produce an already crystallized, multiphase Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 microstructure.
The post-quench sub-Tg intervention may not succeed when the cooling rate is too slow and crystalline phases have already formed.

contradictions.description: The intervention is performed only after rapid quenching and solidification, yet it is claimed to improve amorphous retention during solidification. A post-solidification treatment cannot change retention during the preceding solidification event.
